p: Got it.
So, we’ve investigated many cases, and we’ve confirmed that 16 of those outdoor, non-residential deaths were due to hypo–
[interposing] Were the other three, even though they weren’t due to that, were they identified?
I would have to get back to you on that.
Okay.
But I– we’re quite successful in getting people identified, so I would say likely, but I’ll have to confirm that.
Did OCME observe any trends in the locations or circumstances of these deaths?

Well, there were little differences in terms of the locations across at least four of the five boroughs. Staten Island was relatively spared, but across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Bronx, and Queens there were– there was a relatively even distribution. There was also a relatively even distribution across racial categories in the city. One thing that we did see was that among that group, among that 16, all but one of them were men. And so that was something that wasd noted, and we also– out of the 16, there were 11 of those individuals alcohol and/or drugs or a combination were involved. And so those are some of the meaningful trends that we observed.

During the hearing on Code Blue on– alright. I’m going to talk to you about an issue that’s come up before about emergency vehicles and response times. So, OCME vehicles are currently not eligible to be designated as emergency vehicles with sirens and lights which can delay both

arrival at scenes and return to headquarters. What criteria must OCME vehicles meet to be designated as emergency vehicles, do you know?

This would require that the state, the New York State Vehicles Traffic Law include medical examiner– designate medical examiner’s vehicles to be response vehicles, and if that designation occurs by a change in the state law, we would have the authorization then to have- to be equipped, have our vehicles equipped to be emergency response vehicles. And that is something we’re certainly interested in pursuing. It would help with our response times to scenes, and aside from that, we would be prepared to go forward.
Is the Mayor’s Office– have you had conversations with them about that, or?
We have had conversations around the fact that this is on the legislative agenda.
Okay.
And certainly any suport would be appreciated in that regard.
Sure absolutely. We can talk about that offline. That definitely– how much would it cost to equip every OCME vehicle with an alarm? Do you have that?
I can get back to you with that. We’ve at different points looked at that cost estimate, so we can follow up.
And does OCME have oversight or coordination responsibilities related to EMS response times?
We– I would have to defer to FDNY or EMS on EMS response times.
Are there any steps you’ve taken to support EMS?

I think we work very carefully and closely with EMS in the field, and I think to the extent that we can improve our response times it helps EMS in being able for their teams to get back in service and help others.
Okay. How do delayed response times impact OCME operations and case processing?
Well, really with respect to EMS response times, that doesn’t directly impact–
[interposing] No.

our response. A death occurs, pronounced death by EMS, and then cases are reported to us generally by the police, and then we respond in a coordinated way after that. So, they have minimal impact on us.
Are there staffing or fleet shortages contributing to delays?
Again, I would have to defer to EMS about that.
Okay. what is the total number of OCME’s fleet, and does it motor pool have enough vehicles?
We have 48 vehicles in our fleet, and that is adequate to keep transportation vehicles, investigations vehicles going 24/7/365 at this point.

Okay. So, OCME’s motor pool has a budgeted headcount of 26, but its actual headcount as of January is nine. So, this brings the vacancy rate to 65.4 percent. What are OCME’s efforts to lower the vacancy rates, and what job openings are currently posted?

Well, we have various roles at OCME with respect to who is operating our vehicles. And so that could range from members of our mortuary teams to motor vehicle operators. And as I mentioned earlier, we’ve got a number of vacancies across our forensic operations areas, that we’re in the process of recruiting and hiring for, and so the hope is that that vacancy– those vacancies along with the others we’ve already discussed we’ll be filling.

Okay. I also want to state we’ve been joined by Council Member Ossé. In the Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Budget, OCME has 23 contracts totalling $3.1 million for general maintenance and repairs. Additionally, the plan also includes $210,000 in capital funding for vehicle

replacements. What services are covered under the maintenance and repair contracts?

Those general maintenance and repair contracts are really centered around our facilities. So, three primary areas: facilities and the maintenance and repair of our facilities, IT infrastructure and improvements, and laboratory equipment. So, those three major areas account for that general maintenance and repair budget. IT, IT infrastructure, facilities and laboratory equipment.
What– do any of these contracts include maintenance or repair of OCME vehicles?
No, we work with DCAS with respect to the maintenance and repair for our fleet of vehicles.

So, do you– the question I’m trying to get at, I think, is do you need more vehicles? And the question then becomes instead of doing the maintenance on these vehicles, would newer vehicles cut down that cost and be more efficient or effective?

Well, I think that we– again, we work really closely on keeping our vehicles maintained. We have a fleet of vehicles that has– has a range of ages. Some of those vehicles used more or less frequently, disaster response vehicles, for example, that may not necessarily be in circulation every day, thankfully. And so at the moment, we’re fully capable of responding to scenes on a routine basis in the field as well as in a disaster situation, and at the moment, I see no challenge with respect to having our vehicles maintained and repaired and keeping it–
[interposing] Okay.
fully functional fleet of vehicles in circulation.
We’re just trying to see, because sometimes it’s less, it’s more effective to have a new vehicle as opposed to putting all of the maintenance into something that–
Well, we’ve also had new vehicles added to our fleet in recent times.
Oh, you did, okay.
Yes.

Okay. Alright, thank you. I’m going to go to the Mayor’s Preliminary Management Report. The median time for scene arrivals by medical legal [sic] investigators was two hours and 36 minutes in the first four months of Fiscal 2026, while it took two hours and 25 minutes during the same time period in Fiscal 2025. In addition, the median time for Fiscal 2024, as a whole, was two hours and 13 minutes which in Fiscal 2023 it was one hour and 37 minutes. So, what factors resulted in OCME’s longer scene arrival time?

Well, our scene arrival time is very variable based on several factors. In many instances our scene response is a coordinated effort with the police certainly in suspicious cases or cases that are criminal. There may be a need for crime scene to attend to scene and do their work before we respond. So, there are coordinated efforts that need to go into our response time. I think that’s one factor. Another factor is what we’ve already alluded to in terms of our ability to traverse the entirety of the city, all five

boroughs, dispatching our medical legal investigators from a single location in Manhattan and the ability to navigate depending on the time of day, navigating traffic to get to death scenes across the scene is– has been a factor. Staffing with respect to the number of death investigators that we have that has improved, and so I’m expecting that there’s– and as we continue to hire those positions in forensic operations and expecting our response times to–
[interposing] Go down.
relfect that as well.
Great. We look forward to that. Are there specific neighborhoods that take longer for an investigator to arrive?

Well, I think, you know, again being dispatched centrally from Manhattan there are, you know, the far reaches of the city that we have to attend death scenes, and depending on the time of day, that can be a challenge. But we get to the scenes as quickly as

possible once we’re notified of the death. Again, in that coordinated effort with the other stakeholders.
Okay. Currently the PMMR does not track whether scene arrival times differ when responding to calls at morgues versus private locations. Is this something that you track internally?
Calls in response to–

[interposing] To a body in a morgue versus a private– what I’m getting at, is that it’s emotionally, like, difficult when somebody’s in a private residence or a public location as opposed to you’re picking up a body at a morgue. That’s what I’m–

[interposing] Yeah, absolutely. And that is our– we have a set of triage priorities for cases that are reported to us. Deaths that are in hospitals or nursing homes or other settings that have storage, those are– the cases that are in public view or in people’s homes are top priority for–
[interposing] But do you track the response times for each of those? Do you separate them out?
We do. We do.
Can you get us some of that–
[interposing] Sure.
information? That would be great. Was there a specific event in Fiscal 2025 or Fiscal 2026 that resulted in longer wait times, or again, it’s back to what you were saying earlier?

It’s the same factors that I was mentioning before, and I think there’s also occasionally events that require multiple resources being utilized at a single time that can reflect some of those numbers. For example, response to the Midtown shooting incident which was a complex protracted death scene. And certain instances that require multiple resources can also have an effect statistically on some of those

figures. But primarily, what we were referring to before.

The PMMR indicates that the median time to complete autopsy reports increased by 46 percent in the first four months of Fiscal 2026 compared to the same period in Fiscal 2025, reaching 122.5 days. According to the report, this delay is primarily attributed to the loss of approximately one-third of medical examiner staff due to retirements, recruitment by other jurisdictions and a nationwide shortage of qualified medical examiners. You hired– I think you hired several MEs last year, is that correct?
We did. We–
[interposing] Does the PMMR accurately reflect that you experienced a 33 percent decline with that position?
We’ve lost over the course of two years essentially a third of the medical examiner staff.
Okay.

We have reconstituted that staff by a number of positions. But we’re still, as I’ve testified here before many times now, in the midst of a crisis nationally, and that’s a crisis that we’re not spared of locally. We are doing many things to mitigate that, and I’m pleased with the negotiation that took place on the part of the Doctor’s Council with the city to provide better salaries for our medical examiners, increasing our ability to recruit and retain. We’ve also added locum [sic] tenants [sic] pathologists who are trusted doctors, most of whom we’ve trained who are coming on to support the doctors we have on staff. And we’ve also reorganized in many ways our operations to provide better support to our on-staff doctors to make them more easily able to focus on the work being a medical examiner and reduce their administrative workload in order to produce a reduction in these turnaround times.
We got the OCME salaries increased that time. Are they competitive now, or we still need– have work to do?

They’re far more competitive. I think that this is an ultra-competitive environment when it comes to forensic pathologists. The contract is going to end in 2026, and so I’m hoping additional negotiations will take place around the salary issue in the next contract negotiation.
What’s the starting salary for OCME medical examiners?
Well, the– hiring out of fellowship, I’ll have to get you that detail.
Alright.
But the high end of the salary range for a Board Certified Forensic Pathologist is at $277.
Do you know what the average is around the country?
That has been fluctuating and rising over the past few years, as you might imagine.
Right.
We can provide data on that.
Okay. Just so we have a comparison so we can maybe be helpful there. What is the current size of the autopsy report backlog?
Well, the definition of backlog for me would be those autopsy reports that are not complete after our target turnaround time of 90 days.
Okay.
And so we have– there are a number of those cases, but we’re moving in the right direction. I’ll get back to you on the current number.

Okay, great. Alright. I’m going to talk about the Drug Intelligence and Intervention Group which you mentioned in your opening remarks. The Mayor’s Management Report and Preliminary Mayor’s Management Report tracks agency performance and service delivery across the city since its launch in late 2022.

OCME’s Drug Intelligence and Intervention Group has played a key role in the city’s overdose response by connecting surviving family members and close contacts of individuals who died from overdoses to grief counseling, social services, and treatment referrals. During the first four months of Fiscal 2026, DIIG reached 474 individuals, a 35 percent decrease compared to the same period in Fiscal 2025. The PMMR attributes this decline to an overall reduction in citywide overdose deaths, and a 50 percent staffing reduction. Is DIIG supported by opioid settlement funds, still?
Yes, it is.
How much is allocated to the program, and is the funding time limited or is it ongoing?

I’m very pleased to say that we’ve had $4 million of opioid settlement funding added to our baseline budget, and that will go nowhere. We will have that every year going forward, and that incorporates the DIIG which accounts for 11 headcount in our agency as well as

other areas across the agency that support overdose-related work.
That’s great.
So, we’re pleased that that’s been baselined in our budget.
Are all 11 positions filled or are there some vacant?

We have seven positions filled, and you alluded to a staffing shortage of up to a 50 percent staffing shortage and that was on some levels elevated to a shortage of social workers. One of our family services team who is responsible for outreach to families composed of social workers and other support services, and so the shortage of social workers I think impacted those vacancies. So, we had seven full time people who are on board now, four vacancies, and I’m pleased to also report that those four vacancies we’ve had, we have identified individuals to fill those and are in the process of filling.

Oh, great. Great. By the way, I just want to acknowledge that we’ve been joined by Council Member Gennaro virtually. Do

you have the job titles of these vacant position, or can you get us those?
There are two social workers and two data team members. The specific titles for the data team members we’ll get back to you.
Okay, great. Beyond the decline in overdose deaths and the reported staffing reduction, were there any other factors that contributed to the decrease and individuals reached?
I think that those are the two–
[interposing] Big ones?

primary factors. I think we also, generally speaking, have sometimes challenges in reaching families. We– our DIIG team comes in after we’ve done a death investigation at the scene and we have contact for families, some families wish to talk with us and others may not. And so there are inherent challenges

in doing that outreach work that could affect the number of people we’re able to reach.
Okay. Healthy NYC sets a goal of reducing opioid overdose deaths by 25 percent by 2030. How has DIIG contributed to progress towards that goal?

well, I feel that the rok that that DIIG team is doing and particularly on both th data side, sharing data with partners, stakeholders to be able to use that data to then implement programs and policies in various public health and public safety agencies has been directly contributory. I think even more directly impactful with the respect to the increase of the life expectancy of New Yorkers and saving lives is the work, the outreach work that our family services team are doing to families who are bereaved following a loss of someone toa drug overdose. This is a unique population that has a range of needs across the spectrum of social service needs from suicidal tendencies to substance use issues that need attention, and the work of our social workers and the ability of social workers to contact those folks and

refer them to care is, I think active prevention, lifve-saving work. And so I think that on those levels we have contributed on the part of the DIIG team. And the DIIG team has so also now an even higher level of engagement with families. Now, over 80 percent of the families that we reach, 80 percent, over 80 percent are now accepting services of some sort, be that even grief and bereavement support ranging up to, you know, referral to health care for mental health services or substance use treatment.
What trends is DIIG currently observing in overdose deaths including changes in substances involved or demographic patterns, anything?
Well, while we’re very pleased that we’ve seen a reduction in the number of overdose deaths in the city over the past couple of years. That trend is certainly moving in the right direction.
Right.

However, the overdose crisis is not over. The opioid crisis is not over. We’re still seeing over 2,000 deaths in

the city due to unintentional drug overdose. There has been– and I would defer to the Health Department of the official statistics. But it’s been seeing clearly that areas of the City that are impoverished have disproportionately been impacted. Older Black men have been disproportionately impacted, and while this crisis is still being driven by fentanyl–
[interposing] Right.

We are also continuing to have to monitor what drugs are on the street, what drug combinations are with fentanyl causing these fatalities, and the appearance of new drugs in– on the illicit drug landscape are of consistent concern. The novel benzodiazepines, the synthetic opioids, novel psychoactive substances, wer’e continuously monitoring for those and sharing that data with our partners so people can be aware of what’s going on, on the street, and what combinations of drugs are kiling people.

Okay, no, thank you. Council Member Ossé, you have questions?

COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you so much, Chair, and good morning. Thank you so much for your testimony. My constituents are concerned about the closure of the Crown Heights clinic. I know that this happened last year, but there’s still persistent concerns around its closure. This clinic provided a variety of key health care services that my–
[interposing] Council Member, this is Office of Chief Medical Examiner, not DOHMH. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Oh, DOHMH is not here.
Is later. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: My apologies. I saw the confusion on your face. I will forward my questions.
I can ask them for you if you’d like. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you very much. I appreciate that.
No worries. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you.

Okay. Any other Council Members have questions? No? Thank you very much. Very thoughtful responses. We really appreciate all the work that you do, and I still– you know, I know that you’ve asked us to come out, and we will come out to take a tour at some point. So, thank you.
Anytime. Thank you very much, Chair. Thank you all.
We’re going to be taking a five-minute break, and then we’re going to be doing Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Thank you. [break] [gavel]

Now, I would like to welcome the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene and its Commissioner Dr. Alister Martin. DOHMH’s Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Budget totals $2.51 billion which represents approximately 1.9 percent of the city’s budget. Funding for public health services totals $1.54 billion, a net increase of $57 million compared to last year’s adopted budget. Of

this amount, $503.2 million is for personnel services and just over $1 billion for other than personnel services. However, to echo our concerns with OCME’s budget, the potential impact of federal funding cuts remains significant. The plan as presented reflects a $32.8 million reduction in federal funding compared to the Fiscal 2026 Adopted Budget. We understand that DOHMH typically receives federal grant allocations closer to the middle of the fiscal year which is why these funds are not yet reflected in the Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Budget. However, because federal funding supports a wide range of the city’s public health activities, including disease surveillance, public health infrastructure and prevention programs, we remain concerned about the possibility that some of these funds may not materialize by adoption. Given the ongoing uncertainty surrounding federal public health funding, it is improtant that the city carefully assess potential funding gaps and consider how reductions could affect programs that New Yorkers rely on every day. Several of the msot concerning reductions appear in the disease prevention and

treatment program area, which includes funding for communicable diseases, HIV, immunization, sexually-transferred infections, and tuberculosis programs. The Preliminary Plan reflects a net reduction of $36.7 million compared to Fiscal 2026 adoption. These reductions come at a time when the city is seeing increases in certain communicable diseases. According to the Preliminary Mayor’s Management Report, PMMR, tuberculosis cases rose by 24 percent from 679 cases in calendar year 2023 to 839 in 2024, while new HIV diagnoses increased for the second consecutive year from 1,700 in calendar year 2023 to 1,791 in 2024. The rise in new HIV diagnoses is particularly concerning in light of recent reductions and access to sexual and reproductive health centers in Manhattan closed, potentially limiting access to routine HIV testing and prevention services. Additionally, in late 2024, nonprofit organizations reported shortages of condoms and other safe sex products through the city’s Condom Availability program. Reduced access to both prevention services and protective resources could weaken the city’s HIV prevention efforts at a time

when diagnoses are already increasing. That is why maintaining a strong capacity for disease surveillance, testing and case management remains essential to protecting our public health. We’re also concerned about reductions to programs focused on preventing chronic disease. In the Preliminary Plan, funding for chronic disease preservation within the Center for Health Equity and Community Wellness declined including a $6.4 million reduction in city funding compared to the Fiscal 2026 Adopted Budget and approximately $1 million less in federal funds. Chronic disease remains one of the leading drivers of premature mortality in New York city and sustained investment is critical to improving health outcomes and addressing persistent health inequities across neighborhoods. Vaccination efforts are another area where continued investment will be essential. Vaccination coverage among young children remains below the City’s 70 percent target. According to the PMMR, 63.5 percent of children ages 24 to 35 months were up to date on immunizations in the first quarter of Fiscal 2026. This represents a slight decline from the same period in Fiscal 2025. Ensuring that

the city has sufficient resources for outreach, education, and vaccination access will be imperative ot improving immunization rates. I want to commend you, Commissioner, for the newly-launched media campaign to address vaccine hesitancy. Given the rapid development at the federal level, it is important that DOHMH prepare for a range of potential scenarios. Careful planning will help ensure that the Healthy NYC Initiative to Expand Life Expectancy can continue to move forward and that the city’s public health infrastructure remains strong. Once again, I would like to thank the committees staff and my own staff for this work on this hearing. I also want to acknowledge that we’ve been joined by– I’m going to start over. Okay. We've been joined by Council Member Finance Chair Lee, Council Member Ariola, Council Member Felder, Council Member Ossé, Council Member Aldebol, Council Member Cabán, Council Member Hanks, Gennaro virtual, Narcisse virtual. Okay. I will now turn it over to the Committee Counsel to administer the oath to members of the administration.

Thank you, Chair. Good morning. Please raise your right hands. Do you sweawr to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
Yes.
Yes.
You may proceed with your testimony.

Thank you very much and good morning, Chair Schulman, and good morning Chair Cabán, and Chair Lee and to all the members of the Committee. I’m Dr. Alister Martin, Commissioner of Health at the New York City Health Department and I’m joined today by our Chief Financial Officer Aaron Anderson and members of my senior leadership team. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on our Preliminary Budget as it relates to public health. I’m proud to represent the Mamdani administration which puts forward a vision of a New York City we can all afford. That agenda is not secondary to public health. It is central to it. In our city, one in four New Yorkers are living in poverty. We know that

that has a devastating impact on health. On average, New Yorkers in the poorest parts of our city die nearly seven years earlier than those in our wealthiest neighborhoods. That is seven fewer years to spend with those they love. As we work to design a budget that supports a prosperous New York City, we do that– we do all this work with that in mind. We have our work cut out for us. The data makes it clear that the problems of health and wealth and equity are intimately related, and the good news is that the solutions are, too. Mayor Mamdani’s affordability agenda and our health agenda are aligned. We are focused on buying New Yorkers more time, more health, and more joy in the city we call home. At the New York City Health Department, that work is not new. For decades we have been working at the hyper local level to meet New Yorkers where they are. Every single day we are making systemic changes by building individual connections. In order to change the material conditions of people’s lives at scale, weave to move one conversation at a time. Many of our programs are built on that foundational understanding. For example, the city recently put

$20 million towards the Strong Foundations Initiative which will grow perinatal and early childhood mental health services and expand the Nurse Family Partnership program. I personally have seen firsthand just how meaningful that program in particular is. My mother worked as an NFP nurse for nearly 15 years. I know the impact of that program not by the statistics, but by the children’s books and toys that would pile up in the back of my mom’s old gold Chevy and the stories she told me about mentoring new moms who were considering going back to school or changing careers like she did. A few weeks ago I got to be part of making that announcement about the expansion of services in New York City with my mom in the front row. Public health happens in a million small ways, and it is grounded in relationships we build across our city. All that work taken together contributed to New York City reaching its highest life expectancy in recorded history. That did not happen by accident. Our most recent data shows that 2024 the citywide life expectancy was 83.2 years. That’s higher than pre-pandemic numbers and it’s a testament to a whole of government response to the COVID-19

pandemic, years’ long efforts on overdose prevention and longstanding community work to move the needle on chronic disease. The increase in life span did not happen by accident and it represents a monumental success. That said, we are far from finished. We are still– there are still devastating inequities and life expectancy by race, by neighborhood and by income. We are working to improve health outcomes for New Yorkers harmed by the consequences of historic disinvestment. We know too that we have to interpret these numbers in context. Today’s landscape is entirely different than it was back in 2024. Our latest data show none of the impact of the federal administration’s efforts to sow district, revoke life-saving benefits, and send health care costs soaring. Public health and public services are being dismantled. Yet, we are rocking here maintain our progress in health and longevity of New Yorkers. We stand as a bulwark against misinformation spewing out of Washington, D.C. We have done so since the inauguration of this administration, and we will continue to do so in the months and years ahead. For decades, the New York City Health Department was

closely tethered to national and international public health infrastructure. But in the past year, the United States has adopted an increasingly isolationist approach to international work and a fractured public health strategy domestically. We’re left to fill in gaps as much as possible here in the city. Earlier this year, the United States withdrew from the World Health Organization. In the wake of that decision, we became the first municipal health Department in the country to join the WHO Global Outbreak Alert and Response Network or GOARN. Following an unprecedented overhaul of the federally-recommended childhood vaccination schedule, continue to distribute more than 2.5 million doses of pediatric vaccines to health care providers across our city and to offer clear guidance where the federal government creates confusion. On Monday, a federal court temporarily blocked the CDC’s attempt to change the longstanding childhood vaccination schedule. That is a public health win, but also speaks to the gravity of the federal misinformation we are currently up against without reliable leadership at the CDC, we are creating new avenues

for collaboration and new avenues for information. We continue to work with our regional partners as part of the recently formed Northeast Public Health Collaborative. We’re living in a time of heightened risk and our team is working around the clock to protect the health of New Yorkers and everyone who travels through our great city. That takes a sustained investment from all levels of government and the private sector. I’m now going to turn to the funding that makes all of this work possible. The New York City Health Department has approximately 7,000 employees, all of whom serve more than 8.5 million New Yorkers, 24 hours a day, seven days a week. 2025 marked the third consecutive year in which hiring outpaced staff departures. We are successfully rebuilding our team to full capacity and recovering from staffing shortages caused by pandemic burnout. We have an operating budget of $2 billion for Fiscal Year 2027, about $1 billion of that in City Tax Levy. The remaining billion dollars was sourced from federal and state and private funding. At the city level, we’re grateful to see a continued commitment to public health as we discuss the 2027

Preliminary Budget. In particular, we are encouraged to see resources dedicated to child care site inspections and funding which was also added for outreach and education for early intervention services at 2K sites. In response to the outbreak of legionella in Harlem last summer, additional resources have been appropriated to support more cooling tower inspections, disease surveillance and testing, and community outreach and education. We appreciate the new funding to avert future legionnaire's disease community clusters as much as possible. Additionally, we are happy to provide funding for community-based organizations that serve LGBTQ New Yorkers, especially as federal tax on queer communities continue. And lastly, as a kid from Queens, I’m particularly excited to see start-up funding for a Jamaica Neighborhood Health Action Center to invest in the health of this community. Our brick and mortar presence in priority neighborhoods is a critical part of our work, and I’m encouraged by the resources to expand that model to Queens. At the state level, the Governor’s Fiscal Year 2027 Executive Budget for New York State

provides crucial support for public health. I want to personally thank Governor Kathy Hochul and Commissioner Dr. James McDonald for restoring the Article 6 matching funds of 36 percent to New York City. This reverses several years of cuts when New York City was the only jurisdiction in the state receiving lower state reimbursement for core public health services, despite the fact that we are home to the most individuals with low incomes and the majority of Medicaid recipients in this state. This year, New York State will finally restore parity between New York City and the rest of the state, and I’m deeply grateful for the Governor’s actions on that. I also want to thank Senator Rivera, Assemblymember Gonzalez-Rojas for championing this issue in Albany, and we’re pleased to see the Assembly and Senate include us in their budgets. Finally, thank you to Speaker Menin, to you Chair Schulman, and the entire council for your continued advocacy on this issue. The Health Department also supports Governor Hochul’s proposed plan for universal child care, taxes on tobacco products, and a continued commitment to reproductive health care.

Finally, I’ll speak to the federal budget. About 20 percent of our budget is federally funded. That amounts to approximately $500 million. The majority of that funding goes towards emergency preparedness and infectious disease control. We expect the federal government to honor its commitment and maintain that funding, but if history is any indication, we cannot rely on federal resources. Last spring, the Trump administration unlawfully rescinded $11.4 billion in public health funding. Within that massive cut, approximately $100 million was earmarked for critical disease control and outbreak prevention infrastructure right here at the New York City Health Department. Thankfully, our funding was retained due to a successful lawsuit led by New York State Attorney General Letitia James. That said, we must brace for possible future cuts. We are enduring coordinated and large-scale attacks on public health, and we do not foresee them letting up anytime soon. And so we have a dual responsibility to care for New Yorkers and to serve as a national leader and a universal trusted source in public health. We remain committed to do just

that. I’m very grateful for the support at the state and city levels as we continue to defend public health every single day. I’m confident that even amidst all of these challenges, a healthier more affordable New York City is on the horizon. Thank you for your attention, and we’re happy to take your questions.
Okay, before I ask questions, I’m going to ask Finance Chair Lee for her questions.

Thank you. Good morning. I was going to say afternoon. Sorry. And it’s great to see you, Commissioner, and to see you in person versus just a picture. So, thank you so much for joining us today. So, I’m just going to go right into the Chief Savings Officer plans which I know that we’ve been asking every agency and the Mayor's Executive Order to undertake a Chief Savings Officer and place one at each agency. What was– first, have you identified someone? Who’s the person that you’ve identified, and what was the process to conduct the required review of spending and operations within the 45-day timeframe?

Thank you for that question, Chair. Yeah, we are committed to doing everything we can to comply with this Executive Order and to follow through on the mayor’s vision for the Chief Savings Officer role. Our Chief Savings Officer at this agency is Emiko Otsubo who’s our Chief Operating Officer.
